blocks.text: 4. The fourth sign of stupidity in the ostrich is the very thing that Job presses: that it abandons its eggs and is unmindful of them. Isaiah's ἐπιφώνημα [epiphōnēma] is well known, as if about something impossible, Esa. XLIX, 15. Can a woman forget her offspring, so as not to have compassion on the son of her womb? And the same affection toward offspring has been implanted by nature in the other animals, so that the species may be preserved; it is attributed even to the cetaceans, which are by far the most savage of all animals, Thren. IV, 3. But the ostrich is here excepted, which leaves its eggs on the ground, etc. Hence Damir above: When it leaves the nest to seek food, if it finds the eggs of another ostrich, تحضنه وتنسى بيضها [taḥḍunuhu wa-tansā bayḍahā] it broods on them and forgets its own. And Leo Africanus, book 9: It lays its eggs, ten or twelve in number, in the sand, etc. And since it has a very short memory, it immediately forgets the place. Therefore the female, coming upon these eggs, whether her own or another's, sits on them and warms them. The same is found in Marmol. [II, 867] 5. Finally, among the Arabs, to whom this bird is very well known, we have noted that احمق من النعامة [aḥmaq min al-naʿāma] more foolish than an ostrich is said for "most foolish." The very build of its body amply shows this. For it has a very small head and almost no brain. Hence in Arabic it is called صعون [ṣaʿwan] sivvan, that is, الدقيق العنق والصغير الراس او العام [al-daqīq al-ʿunuq wa-al-ṣaghīr al-rās aw al-ʿām] thin of neck and small of head, or of crown. It is also called انقخ [anqakh] ankach, that is, قليل الدماغ [qalīl al-dimāgh] of little brain. So Alcamus. For this reason Heliogabalus served the heads of six hundred ostriches at a single dinner, so that their little brains might be eaten. So many were needed for there to be plenty for the guests, since individual ostriches have hardly any brain. Further, the head of the ostrich, carried on a long thin neck, cannot be steady. That is why they call the animal itself نغض [nighḍ] nigd, because نغض [naghaḍa] nagada means to nod the head. Again Alcamus: نغض اسم الظليم معرفة للجوال منه [nighḍ ism al-ẓalīm maʿrifa lil-jawwāl minhu] Nigd, a name of the ostrich, given to it from its agitation. And on the same word Damir: الظليم سمي بذلك لانه يحرك راسه [al-ẓalīm summiya bi-dhālika li-annahu yuḥarriku rasahu] The ostrich is so called because it moves its head. With such agitation of the head the imaginative faculty can hardly be steady and keep to its own level. And since the ear, even in brute animals, is in its own way the sense of learning, in the ostrich stupidity is increased by deafness, which is natural to it. Khalawayh, in the book ليس [laysa] Laisa, or There is not (which we said is On things that are lacking to someone, or somewhere): ليس في الدنيا حيوان لا يسمع الا النعام [laysa fī al-dunyā ḥayawān lā yasmaʿu illā al-naʿām] There is no animal in the world (no perfect animal) that does not hear, except the ostrich. [col. 261] Leo Africanus, book 9: The ostrich is a simple and deaf animal. Marmol: El abestruez es simple, y sordò, que no oye cosa ninguna. All this sheds light on these words of Job: God has deprived her of wisdom, etc. It remains to explain the last words of the sacred writer, who closes the description of the ostrich thus:
